terms.definition: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes.
The three main components of the scientific attitude; the passion to explore, the refusal to accept claims without evidence, and the willingness to admit when one is wrong.
Thinking that does not blindly accept arguments and conclusions; rather, it examines assumptions, discerns hidden values, evaluates evidence, and assesses conclusions.
The tendency to believe, after learning an outcome, that one would have foreseen it (also known as the "I-knew-it-all-along" phenomenon).
A tendency to search for information that supports our preconceptions and to ignore or distort contradictory evidence.
The tendency to be more confident than correct—to overestimate the accuracy of our beliefs and judgments.
Scientific experts who evaluate a research article's theory, originality, and accuracy before it is published to ensure quality.
An explanation using an integrated set of principles that organizes observations and predicts behaviors or events.
A testable prediction, often implied by a theory.
A carefully worded statement of the exact procedures (operations) used in a research study so that it can be replicated.
Repeating the essence of a research study, usually with different participants in different situations, to see whether the basic finding extends to other participants and circumstances.
A descriptive technique in which one individual or group is studied in depth in the hope of revealing universal principles.
A statistical procedure for analyzing the results of multiple studies to reach an overall conclusion.
Observing and recording behavior in naturally occurring situations without trying to manipulate and control the situation.
A technique for ascertaining the self-reported attitudes or behaviors of a particular group, usually by questioning a representative, random sample of the group.
The tendency for survey participants to answer questions in a manner that will be viewed favorably by others rather than truthfully.
A methodological problem that arises when researchers rely on participants to give their own accounts of their behaviors or feelings, which may be inaccurate.
The influence of the experimenter's expectations or preferences on the outcome of a research study.
All those in a group being studied, from which samples may be drawn.
A subset of individuals chosen from a larger set (a population).
A flawed sampling process that produces an unrepresentative sample.
A sample that fairly represents a population because each member has an equal chance of inclusion.
A sample that accurately reflects the characteristics of the population as a whole.
Research methods involving the manipulation of one or more variables to determine cause and effect.
Research methods that do not involve manipulation of independent variables (e.g., observation, correlation, case studies).
A measure of the extent to which two variables change together, and thus of how well either variable predicts the other.
A statistical index of the relationship between two variables (from -1.0 to +1.0).
Anything that can vary and is feasible and ethical to measure.
A graphed cluster of dots, each of which represents the values of two variables. The slope suggests the direction of the relationship.
The perception of a relationship where none exists, or perceiving a stronger-than-actual relationship.
The situation in correlational research where it is known that two variables are related, but it is unclear which variable is causing the other.
The tendency for extreme or unusual scores to fall back (regress) toward their average.
A research method in which an investigator manipulates one or more factors (independent variables) to observe the effect on some behavior or mental process (the dependent variable).
In an experiment, the group exposed to the treatment, that is, to one version of the independent variable.
In an experiment, the group not exposed to the treatment; contrasts with the experimental group and serves as a comparison.
The experimental factor that is manipulated; the variable whose effect is being studied.
The outcome factor; the variable that may change in response to manipulations of the independent variable.
Assigning participants to experimental and control groups by chance, thus minimizing preexisting differences between the different groups.
An experimental procedure in which the research participants are ignorant (blind) about whether they have received the treatment or a placebo.
An experimental procedure in which both the research participants and the research staff are ignorant (blind) about whether the research participants have received the treatment or a placebo.
An inert substance or condition that may be administered instead of a presumed active agent, such as a drug, to see if it triggers the effects believed to characterize the active agent.
A factor other than the independent variable that might produce an effect in an experiment.
Research that translates the social world into numbers that can be treated mathematically.
Research that focuses on non-numerical data, such as subjective experiences, feelings, or beliefs.
A psychometric scale commonly involved in research that employs questionnaires (e.g., "Strongly Agree" to "Strongly Disagree").
An administrative body (IRB) established to protect the rights and welfare of human research subjects recruited to participate in research activities.
An ethical principle that research participants be told enough to enable them to choose whether they wish to participate.
The ethical requirement that researchers ensure participants do not suffer undue physical or psychological harm during the study.
The ethical principle that personal information obtained from a participant in research or therapy should not be revealed without the individual's permission.
The post-experimental explanation of a study, including its purpose and any deceptions, to its participants.
Numerical data used to measure and describe characteristics of groups. Includes measures of central tendency and measures of variation.
A bar graph depicting a frequency distribution.
A single score that represents a whole set of scores (e.g., mean, median, mode).
The most frequently occurring score(s) in a distribution.
The arithmetic average of a distribution, obtained by adding the scores and then dividing by the number of scores.
The middle score in a distribution; half the scores are above it and half are below it.
The percentage of scores that fall below a specific score in a distribution.
A representation of scores that lack symmetry around their average value (e.g., a long tail on one side).
Tools used to describe the distribution or dispersion of data (e.g., range, standard deviation).
The difference between the highest and lowest scores in a distribution.
A computed measure of how much scores vary around the mean score.
A symmetrical, bell-shaped curve that describes the distribution of many types of data; most scores fall near the mean.
Numerical data that allow one to generalize—to infer from sample data the probability of something being true of a population.
A statistical statement of how likely it is that an obtained result occurred by chance (typically p < 0.05).
A measure of the strength of the relationship between two variables or the extent of an experimental effect.
A branch of psychology that links biological (genetic, neural, hormonal) and psychological processes.
A branch of psychology that studies how unconscious drives and conflicts influence behavior, and uses that information to treat people with psychological disorders.
The scientific study of observable behavior, and its explanation by principles of learning (e.g., conditioning, reinforcement).
The scientific study of all the mental activities associated with thinking, knowing, remembering, and communicating.
A perspective that emphasizes the growth potential of healthy people and the individual's potential for personal growth.
The study of how situations and cultures affect our behavior and thinking.
An integrated approach that incorporates biological, psychological, and social-cultural levels of analysis.
The genetic transfer of characteristics from parents to offspring.
The influence of our inherited characteristics (genetics) on personality, physical growth, and social interactions.
The influence of environmental factors such as family, culture, and experience on development.
An increased likelihood of developing a particular disease or trait based on a person's genetic makeup.
The study of the evolution of behavior and the mind, using principles of natural selection.
The principle that traits leading to increased reproduction and survival will most likely be passed on to succeeding generations.
The controversial practice or advocacy of improving the human species by selectively mating people with specific desirable hereditary traits.
Research that compares identical (monozygotic) and fraternal (dizygotic) twins to determine the relative contribution of genes vs. environment.
The complex of nerve tissues that controls the activities of the body, comprising the brain and spinal cord.
The sensory and motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls the glands and the muscles of the internal organs (such as the heart).
The division of the autonomic nervous system that arouses the body, mobilizing its energy in stressful situations (Fight or Flight).
The division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body, conserving its energy (Rest and Digest).
The division of the peripheral nervous system that controls the body's skeletal muscles (voluntary movements).
Nerve cells; the basic building block of the nervous system.
Cells in the nervous system that support, nourish, and protect neurons; they also play a role in learning and thinking.
A neural pathway that controls a reflex, involving sensory neurons, interneurons in the spinal cord, and motor neurons.
Neurons that carry incoming information from the sensory receptors to the brain and spinal cord (Afferent).
Neurons that carry outgoing information from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles and glands (Efferent).
Neurons within the brain and spinal cord that communicate internally and intervene between the sensory inputs and motor outputs.
The process by which signaling molecules called neurotransmitters are released by a neuron and bind to and activate the receptors of another neuron.
A neural impulse; a brief electrical charge that travels down an axon.
A neuron’s reaction of either firing (with a full-strength response) or not firing.
The process during the action potential when sodium is rushing into the cell causing the interior to become more positive.
A period of inactivity after a neuron has fired, during which it cannot fire again until it resets.
The positive-outside/negative-inside state of the axon membrane when a neuron is not firing.
A neurotransmitter's reabsorption by the sending neuron.
The level of stimulation required to trigger a neural impulse.
A disease in which the immune system eats away at the protective covering (myelin sheath) of nerves, slowing communication.
A weakness and rapid fatigue of muscles under voluntary control caused by a breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles.
Chemicals that stimulate the next neuron to fire.
Chemicals that decrease the likelihood that the next neuron will fire.
Influences movement, learning, attention, and emotion; excess linked to schizophrenia, starved linked to Parkinson’s.
Affects mood, hunger, sleep, and arousal; undersupply linked to depression.
Helps control alertness and arousal; undersupply can depress mood.
A major excitatory neurotransmitter; involved in memory.
A major inhibitory neurotransmitter; undersupply linked to seizures and insomnia.
"Morphine within"—natural, opiate-like neurotransmitters linked to pain control and to pleasure.
A neurotransmitter involved in the transmission of pain messages to the brain.
Enables muscle action, learning, and memory; deterioration of ACh-producing neurons leads to Alzheimer’s.
Chemical messengers that are manufactured by the endocrine glands, travel through the bloodstream, and affect other tissues.
A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands, especially in conditions of stress, increasing rates of blood circulation and breathing.
A hormone produced by fat cells that acts as a satiety factor in regulating appetite.
A hormone secreted by an empty stomach that sends "I'm hungry" signals to the brain.
A hormone manufactured by the pineal gland that produces sleepiness.
A hormone released by the pituitary gland that causes increased contraction of the uterus during labor and stimulates the ejection of milk; also linked to social bonding.
Chemical substances that alter perceptions and moods.
Molecules that increase a neurotransmitter's action.
Molecules that inhibit or block a neurotransmitter's action.
Drugs that block the reabsorption of neurotransmitters by the presynaptic neuron, increasing their concentration in the synapse.
Drugs (such as caffeine, nicotine, and the more powerful amphetamines, cocaine, and Ecstasy) that excite neural activity and speed up body functions.
A stimulant drug found in coffee, tea, and soda that increases alertness.
A powerful and addictive stimulant, derived from the coca plant, producing temporarily increased alertness and euphoria.
Drugs (such as alcohol, barbiturates, and opiates) that reduce neural activity and slow body functions.
A depressant that slows the central nervous system, reduces inhibitions, and impairs judgment.
Psychedelic drugs, such as LSD, that distort perceptions and evoke sensory images in the absence of sensory input.
A mild hallucinogen that can amplify sensitivity to colors, sounds, tastes, and smells, but also relax and disinhibit.
Opium and its derivatives, such as morphine and heroin; they depress neural activity, temporarily lessening pain and anxiety.
A highly addictive analgesic drug derived from morphine, often used illicitly as a narcotic.
The diminishing effect with regular use of the same dose of a drug, requiring the user to take larger and larger doses to experience the effect.
Compulsive craving of drugs or certain behaviors (such as gambling) despite known adverse consequences.
The discomfort and distress that follow discontinuing an addictive drug or behavior.
The oldest part and central core of the brain, beginning where the spinal cord swells as it enters the skull; responsible for automatic survival functions.
The base of the brainstem; controls heartbeat and breathing.
A nerve network in the brainstem that plays an important role in controlling arousal and sleep/wake transitions.
A dopamine-rich pathway in the brain (including the nucleus accumbens) that rewards activities essential to survival.
The "little brain" at the rear of the brainstem; functions include processing sensory input, coordinating movement output, and balance.
The intricate fabric of interconnected neural cells covering the cerebral hemispheres; the body's ultimate control and information-processing center.
Neural system located below the cerebral hemispheres; associated with emotions and drives.
The brain's sensory control center, located on top of the brainstem; it directs messages to the sensory receiving areas in the cortex.
A neural structure below the thalamus; directs eating, drinking, body temperature, and helps govern the endocrine system via the pituitary gland.
The endocrine system's most influential gland (Master Gland). Under the influence of the hypothalamus, it regulates growth and controls other glands.
A neural center located in the limbic system that helps process explicit memories for storage.
Two lima-bean-sized neural clusters in the limbic system; linked to emotion, specifically fear and aggression.
The large band of neural fibers connecting the two brain hemispheres and carrying messages between them.
Portion of the cerebral cortex lying at the back of the head; includes areas that receive information from the visual fields.
Portion of the cerebral cortex lying roughly above the ears; includes the auditory areas.
Portion of the cerebral cortex lying at the top of the head and toward the rear; receives sensory input for touch and body position.
Areas of the cerebral cortex that are not involved in primary motor or sensory functions; rather, they are involved in higher mental functions.
Area at the front of the parietal lobes that registers and processes body touch and movement sensations.
Portion of the cerebral cortex lying just behind the forehead; involved in speaking, muscle movements, and in making plans and judgments.
The brain's ability to understand and produce language, primarily centered in the left hemisphere.
Complex cognitive processes such as analysis, synthesis, evaluation, and creation.
Cognitive processes that include working memory, flexible thinking, and self-control.
The forward part of the frontal lobes responsible for judgment, planning, and processing new memories.
An area at the rear of the frontal lobes that controls voluntary movements.
Study of patients with severed corpus callosum; shows that the two hemispheres can operate independently.
The tendency of some cognitive functions to be specialized to either the left or right hemisphere.
Controls language expression—an area of the frontal lobe, usually in the left hemisphere, that directs the muscle movements involved in speech.
Controls language reception—a brain area involved in language comprehension and expression; usually in the left temporal lobe.
Impairment of language, usually caused by left hemisphere damage either to Broca’s area (impairing speaking) or to Wernicke’s area (impairing understanding).
The concept that the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body, and the right hemisphere controls the left side.
The brain’s ability to change, especially during childhood, by reorganizing after damage or by building new pathways based on experience.
Electroencephalogram; an amplified recording of the waves of electrical activity sweeping across the brain's surface.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging; a technique for revealing blood flow and, therefore, brain activity by comparing successive MRI scans.
Tissue destruction. A brain lesion is a naturally or experimentally caused destruction of brain tissue.
Our awareness of ourselves and our environment.
The biological clock; regular bodily rhythms that occur on a 24-hour cycle.
Fatigue and sleep disturbance resulting from disruption of the body's normal circadian rhythm following long flights through different time zones.
Work schedules that take place outside the traditional 9-to-5 day, often disrupting circadian rhythms and sleep patterns.
The transition period between wakefulness and sleep; characterized by theta waves and potential hypnogogic sensations.
Bizarre experiences, such as jerking or a feeling of falling or floating weightlessly, while transitioning to sleep.
Deeper sleep characterized by sleep spindles (bursts of rapid, rhythmic brain-wave activity).
Deep sleep stage characterized by large, slow delta waves.
Rapid eye movement sleep; a recurring sleep stage during which vivid dreams commonly occur. Also known as paradoxical sleep.
The tendency for REM sleep to increase following REM sleep deprivation.
The theory that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity occurring during sleep.
The theory that dreams help us sort out the day's events and consolidate our memories.
The neural process by which a temporary memory is converted into a stable, long-term form.
The theory that sleep allows the body and brain to recover from the day's physical and mental exertion.
Recurring problems in falling or staying asleep.
A sleep disorder characterized by uncontrollable sleep attacks; the sufferer may lapse directly into REM sleep.
A sleep disorder in which you physically act out vivid, often unpleasant dreams with vocal sounds and sudden, often violent arm and leg movements.
A sleep disorder characterized by temporary cessations of breathing during sleep and repeated momentary awakenings.
Sleepwalking; occurs during NREM-3 deep sleep.
The process by which our sensory receptors and nervous system receive and represent stimulus energies from our environment.
Conversion of one form of energy into another. In sensation, the transforming of stimulus energies into neural impulses our brain can interpret.
The minimum stimulus energy needed to detect a particular stimulus 50 percent of the time.
The minimum difference between two stimuli required for detection 50 percent of the time (also called the difference threshold).
Diminished sensitivity as a consequence of constant stimulation.
The principle that, to be perceived as different, two stimuli must differ by a constant minimum percentage (rather than a constant amount).
The principle that one sense may influence another, as when the smell of food influences its taste.
A condition in which one sense is simultaneously perceived as if by one or more additional senses such as sight.
The light-sensitive inner surface of the eye, containing the receptor rods and cones plus layers of neurons that begin the processing of visual information.
The point at which the optic nerve leaves the eye where there are no receptor cells
The nerve that carries neural impulses from the eye to the brain.
The transparent structure behind the pupil that changes shape to help focus images on the retina.
The process by which the eye's lens changes shape to focus near or far objects on the retina.
A condition in which nearby objects are seen more clearly than distant objects because distant objects focus in front of the retina.
A condition in which faraway objects are seen more clearly than near objects because the image of near objects is focused behind the retina.
Cells in the retina that respond to light; includes rods and cones.
Retinal receptors that detect black, white, and gray; necessary for peripheral and twilight vision, when cones don’t respond.
Retinal receptor cells that are concentrated near the center of the retina and that function in daylight or in well-lit conditions. They detect fine detail and give rise to color sensations.

The theory that the retina contains three different color receptors—one most sensitive to red, one to green, one to blue—which, when stimulated in combination, can produce the perception of any color.
The theory that opposing retinal processes (red-green, yellow-blue, white-black) enable color vision.
Visual images that remain after removal of or looking away from the stimulus (often explained by opponent-process theory).
Specialized neurons in the retina that both connect to the bipolar cells and form the optic nerve
A form of color blindness in which only two of the three primary colors can be perceived.
Total color blindness; the inability to distinguish any colors.
A cognitive disorder of face perception in which the ability to recognize familiar faces, including one's own face, is impaired.
A condition in which a person can respond to a visual stimulus without consciously experiencing it.
The distance from the peak of one light or sound wave to the peak of the next.
A tone's experienced highness or lowness; depends on frequency.
The height of a wave; determines the intensity/brightness of light and the loudness of sound.
Our perception of the intensity of a sound, measured in decibels.
The process by which the ear and brain interpret the frequency of sound waves.
In hearing, the theory that links the pitch we hear with the location where the cochlea's membrane is stimulated
A theory of hearing which states that groups of neurons of the auditory system respond to a sound by firing action potentials slightly out of phase with one another.
In hearing, the theory that the rate of nerve impulses traveling up the auditory nerve matches the frequency of a tone, thus enabling us to sense its pitch.
The process by which the brain identifies the location of a sound source.
Hearing loss caused by damage to the mechanical system that conducts sound waves to the cochlea.
Hearing loss caused by damage to the cochlea's receptor cells or to the auditory nerves; also called nerve deafness.
The sensory system used for smelling.
Chemical signals released by an animal that communicate information and affect the behavior of other animals of the same species.
The physical act of tasting.
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami (savory), and oleogustus (fatty).
Specialized parts of taste buds where transduction occurs
People who have more taste buds than average and are extra sensitive to flavors.
People with an average number of taste buds.
People with fewer taste buds who are less sensitive to flavors.
The principle that one sense may influence another, such as how smell affects taste.
The theory that the spinal cord contains a neurological "gate" that blocks pain signals or allows them to pass on to the brain.
The sensation that an amputated or missing limb is still attached.
The sense of body movement and position, including the sense of balance (controlled by semicircular canals in the ear).
Three fluid-filled canals in the inner ear that help maintain balance by detecting rotation.
The system for sensing the position and movement of individual body parts.
Analysis that begins with the sensory receptors and works up to the brain's integration of sensory information.
Information processing guided by higher-level mental processes, drawing on experience and expectations.
A framework that organizes and interprets information.
A mental predisposition to perceive one thing and not another.
Emphasizes our tendency to integrate pieces of information into meaningful wholes.
The Gestalt principle where the brain fills in gaps to create a complete, whole object.
The organization of the visual field into objects (figures) that stand out from their surroundings (ground).
Gestalt principle where we group nearby figures together.
Gestalt principle where we group similar figures together.
The processing of a limited amount of information from the enormous amount available.
The focusing of conscious awareness on a particular stimulus.
Ability to attend to only one voice among many while also being able to detect your own name.
Failing to see visible objects when our attention is directed elsewhere.
Failing to notice changes in the environment.
Depth cues that depend on the use of two eyes.
A binocular cue for perceiving depth by comparing images from the retinas in the two eyes.
A binocular cue; the extent to which the eyes move inward when looking at an object.
Depth cues available to either eye alone (e.g., relative size, interposition).
Monocular cue; hazy objects are seen as farther away than sharp, clear objects.
Monocular cue; if two objects are similar in size, the one that casts the smaller retinal image is farther away.
Monocular cue; a gradual change from a coarse distinct texture to a fine, indistinct texture signals distance.
Monocular cue; parallel lines appear to meet in the distance.
Monocular cue; if one object partially blocks our view of another, we perceive it as closer.
The perception of movement in stationary objects (e.g., phi phenomenon).
A mental image or best example of a category.
Mental frameworks that help organize and interpret information.
Interpreting our new experiences in terms of our existing schemas.
Adapting our current understandings (schemas) to incorporate new information.
A methodical, logical rule or procedure that guarantees solving a particular problem.
A simple thinking strategy that often allows us to make judgments and solve problems efficiently.
Judging the likelihood of things in terms of how well they seem to represent, or match, particular prototypes.
Estimating the likelihood of events based on their availability in memory.
A tendency to approach a problem in one particular way, often a way that has been successful in the past.
The activation, often unconsciously, of certain associations, thus predisposing one's perception or memory.
The way an issue is posed; how an issue is framed can significantly affect decisions and judgments.
The belief that the chance of a random event occurring is influenced by previous instances of that event.
Continuing an endeavor as a result of previously invested resources (time, money, or effort).
Higher-order mental processes (planning, decision making) handled by the frontal lobe.
The ability to produce novel and valuable ideas.
Expanding the number of possible problem solutions; creative thinking.
Narrowing the available problem solutions to determine the single best solution.
The tendency to think of things only in terms of their usual functions.
The process of retaining encoded information over time.
The process of getting information out of memory storage.
Memory of facts and experiences that one can consciously know and "declare."
Explicit memory of personally experienced events.
Explicit memory of facts and general knowledge.
Retention of learned skills or classically conditioned associations independent of conscious recollection.
Implicit memory for cognitive and motor skills (e.g., riding a bike).
Remembering to do things in the future.
An increase in a cell's firing potential after brief, rapid stimulation; believed to be a neural basis for learning.
Baddeley's model of memory that includes the central executive, phonological loop, and sketchpad.
Active processing of incoming auditory and visual-spatial information, and information retrieved from LTM.
The "manager" of working memory that directs attention and coordinates subsystems.
Part of working memory that deals with spoken and written material.
Part of working memory that deals with visual and spatial information.
The relatively permanent and limitless storehouse of the memory system.
Atkinson-Shiffrin model: Sensory -> Short Term -> Long Term.
The immediate, very brief recording of sensory information in the memory system.
A momentary sensory memory of visual stimuli.
A momentary sensory memory of auditory stimuli.
Unconscious encoding of incidental information.
Encoding that requires attention and conscious effort.
The processing of information into the memory system.
Craik and Lockhart’s theory that how deeply we process info determines how well it is remembered.
Encoding on a basic level based on the structure or appearance of words.
Encoding semantically, based on the meaning of the words; yields the best retention.
The three levels of processing: appearance, sound, and meaning.
Memory aids, especially those techniques that use vivid imagery and organizational devices.
A mnemonic technique that involves associating items with a sequence of familiar physical locations.
Organizing items into familiar, manageable units; often occurs automatically.
Grouping objects or ideas based on shared properties.
Organizing information from broad concepts to narrower, more specific details.
The tendency for distributed study or practice to yield better long-term retention than massed practice.
The neural storage of a long-term memory.
Cramming; producing speedy short-term learning but poor long-term retention.
Spacing out study sessions over time.
Our tendency to recall best the last and first items in a list.
Better recall for items at the beginning of a list.
Better recall for items at the end of a list.
Repeating information over and over to keep it in short-term memory.
Thinking about the meaning of the term to be remembered, as opposed to simply repeating it.
The proportion of material retained (remembered).
Memory system consisting of episodes recollected from an individual's life.
An inability to retrieve information from one's past.
An inability to form new memories.
A progressive brain disorder that slowly destroys memory and thinking skills.
The inability of adults to retrieve episodic memories before the age of 2-4 years.
Retrieving information that is not currently in your conscious awareness (e.g., fill-in-the-blank test).
Identifying items previously learned (e.g., multiple-choice test).
External information that is associated with stored information and helps bring it to mind.
Improved recall of specific information when the context present at encoding and retrieval are the same.
The tendency to recall experiences that are consistent with one's current good or bad mood.
What we learn in one state (drunk/sober) may be more easily recalled when we are again in that state.
Enhanced memory after retrieving, rather than simply rereading, information.
Thinking about thinking; awareness and understanding of one's own thought processes.
Ebbinghaus's finding that the course of forgetting is initially rapid, then levels off with time.
Failure to process information into memory.
The disruptive effect of prior learning on the recall of new information.
The disruptive effect of new learning on the recall of old information.
The temporary inability to retrieve a word that is well known to the person.
In psychoanalytic theory, the basic defense mechanism that banishes anxiety-arousing thoughts from consciousness.
Incorporating misleading information into one's memory of an event.
Attributing to the wrong source an event we have experienced, heard about, or imagined.
An apparent memory of an event that did not actually happen, built from various sources.
The finding that imagining an event which never happened can increase confidence that it actually occurred.
Mental quality consisting of the ability to learn from experience, solve problems, and use knowledge to adapt.
The common cognitive abilities underlying performance across various mental tasks
Our ability to reason speedily and abstractly; tends to decrease during late adulthood.
Defined originally as the ratio of mental age to chronological age multiplied by 100.
The level of performance typically associated with a certain age.
The actual age of the person.
Defining uniform testing procedures and meaningful scores by comparison with the performance of a pretested group.
The extent to which a test measures or predicts what it is supposed to.
The degree to which a test measures what it claims to be measuring.
The success with which a test predicts the behavior it is designed to predict.
The extent to which a test yields consistent results.
Using the same test on two occasions to measure consistency.
Dividing the test into two comparable halves and seeing if scores correlate.
A self-confirming concern that one will be evaluated based on a negative stereotype.
Performance boost caused by the awareness of a positive stereotype of one's group.
The substantial and long-sustained increase in both fluid and crystallized intelligence test scores measured in many parts of the world.
Tests designed to assess what a person has learned.
Tests designed to predict a person's future performance
The idea that our abilities are innate and cannot be changed.
The idea that our abilities are malleable qualities that we can cultivate and grow.
The study of age-related changes as they occur over time throughout the lifespan.
The field of study that examines patterns of growth, change, and stability in behavior that occur throughout the entire human life cycle.
The debate regarding whether early personality traits persist through life or if people become different individuals as they age.
The long-standing controversy over the relative contributions that genes and experience make to the development of psychological traits and behaviors.
The view that development is a gradual, cumulative process of expanding upon existing skills.
The view that development takes place in unique stages, occurring at specific times or ages.
Agents, such as chemicals and viruses, that can reach the embryo or fetus during prenatal development and cause harm.
The control and precision of small muscle movements, such as those in the hands and fingers.
The control and movement of large muscle groups, such as those used for walking or jumping.
Biological growth processes that enable orderly changes in behavior, relatively uninfluenced by experience.
Unlearned, organized involuntary responses that occur automatically in the presence of certain stimuli.
A baby's tendency, when touched on the cheek, to turn toward the touch and open the mouth in search of a nipple.
A laboratory device used for testing depth perception in infants and young animals.
An optimal period early in the life of an organism when exposure to certain stimuli or experiences produces normal development.
A time that is optimal for certain capacities to emerge and in which the individual is especially responsive to environmental influences.
The process by which certain animals form strong attachments during an early-life critical period.
A rapid increase in height and weight that typically occurs during puberty.
The period of sexual maturation, during which a person becomes capable of reproducing.
The body structures (ovaries, testes, and external genitalia) that make sexual reproduction possible.
Nonreproductive sexual characteristics, such as female breasts and hips, male voice quality, and body hair.
The first menstrual period in a female.
A male's first ejaculation.
The time of natural cessation of menstruation; also refers to the biological changes a woman experiences as her ability to reproduce declines.
Concepts or mental frameworks that organize and interpret information.
Interpreting our new experiences in terms of our existing schemas.
Adapting our current understandings (schemas) to incorporate new information.
Piaget's first stage (birth to ~2 years) during which infants know the world mostly in terms of sensory impressions and motor activities.
The awareness that things continue to exist even when not perceived.
Piaget's second stage (~2 to 6/7 years) during which a child learns to use language but does not yet comprehend the mental operations of concrete logic.
Internal depictions of information that the mind can manipulate (e.g., images and concepts).
Play in which children use objects or actions to represent something else (symbolic function).
The principle that properties such as mass, volume, and number remain the same despite changes in the forms of objects.
The capacity to think through a series of steps and then mentally reverse direction, returning to the starting point.
The belief that inanimate objects have lifelike qualities, such as thoughts and feelings.
In Piaget's theory, the preoperational child's difficulty taking another's point of view.
People's ideas about their own and others' mental states—about their feelings, perceptions, and thoughts, and the behaviors these might predict.
Piaget's third stage (~7 to 11 years) during which children gain the mental operations that enable them to think logically about concrete events.
The ability to process information in a logical and organized manner.
Piaget's final stage (beginning ~age 12) during which people begin to think logically about abstract concepts.
The ability to understand concepts that are not directly tied to physical objects or experiences.
The ability to reason about "what if" scenarios and possibilities that may not be real.
A process in which more skilled individuals provide temporary support to a learner, tapering it off as the learner's competence increases.
In Vygotsky's theory, the range between children's present level of knowledge and their potential knowledge state if they receive help.
Our accumulated knowledge and verbal skills; tends to increase with age.
Our ability to reason speedily and abstractly; tends to decrease during late adulthood.
An abnormal condition marked by multiple cognitive defects that include memory impairment.
In language, the smallest distinctive sound unit.
In language, the smallest unit that carries meaning; may be a word or a part of a word (such as a prefix).
The set of rules by which we derive meaning from morphemes, words, and sentences in a given language.
In a language, a system of rules that enables us to communicate with and understand others.
The rules for combining words into grammatically sensible sentences in a given language.
Spontaneous making of vowel-like sounds by infants (around 2 months).
Stage of language development at about 4 months when an infant spontaneously utters various sounds.
The stage in speech development, from about age 1 to 2, during which a child speaks mostly in single words.
Early speech stage in which a child speaks using mostly nouns and verbs (go car)
A grammatical error in which children apply a language rule too broadly (e.g., "I goed to the park").
Bronfenbrenner's model which views the person as developing within a complex system of relationships affected by multiple levels of the surrounding environment.
The immediate environment that an individual interacts with directly (e.g., family, school).
The connections between various microsystems (e.g., the relationship between a child's parents and their teacher).
Social settings that a person may not experience firsthand but that still influence development (e.g., a parent's workplace).
The larger cultural context, including values, laws, and resources.
The dimension of time in relation to a person's development, including life transitions and historical events.
A restrictive, punitive style of parenting in which parents exhort the child to follow their directions and respect their work and effort.
A parenting style that encourages children to be independent but still places limits and controls on their actions.
A style of parenting in which parents are very involved with their children but place few demands or controls on them.
The expectations people develop about relationships with others, based on the relationship they had with their primary caregiver.
A relationship in which an infant obtains both comfort and confidence from the presence of his or her caregiver.
Attachments marked by anxiety or ambivalence; infants are less likely to explore and may cling to or avoid the caregiver.
Infants who seem unresponsive to the parent when they are present and are usually not distressed when she leaves.
A style where the child is distressed when the caregiver leaves and remains distressed or angry upon their return.
A type of attachment that is marked by an infant's inconsistent or confused reactions to the caregiver's departure and return.
A person's characteristic emotional reactivity and intensity.
Emotional distress seen in many infants when they are separated from people with whom they have formed an attachment.
Activity in which children play side by side without interacting.
Adolescents' belief that others are as interested in them as they itself are; the feeling of being "on stage."
The part of adolescent egocentrism that involves an adolescent's sense of uniqueness and invincibility.
The culturally preferred timing of social events such as marriage, parenthood, and retirement.
A period from the late teens to mid-twenties, bridging the gap between adolescent dependence and full adult independence and responsibility.
A comprehensive theory consisting of eight stages of psychosocial development, each characterized by a specific crisis.
Erikson's first stage (0-1 yr): If needs are dependably met, infants develop a sense of basic trust.
Erikson's second stage (1-3 yrs): Toddlers learn to exercise their will and do things for themselves, or they doubt their abilities.
Erikson's third stage (3-6 yrs): Preschoolers learn to initiate tasks and carry out plans, or they feel guilty about their efforts to be independent.
Erikson's fourth stage (6-puberty): Children learn the pleasure of applying themselves to tasks, or they feel inferior.
Erikson's fifth stage (adolescence): Teenagers work at refining a sense of self by testing roles, or they become confused about who they are.
Erikson's sixth stage (young adulthood): Individuals form close relationships and gain the capacity for intimate love, or they feel socially isolated.
Erikson's seventh stage (middle adulthood): People discover a sense of contributing to the world, or they may feel a lack of purpose.
Erikson's eighth stage (late adulthood): Reflecting on one's life, an older adult may feel a sense of satisfaction or failure.
Potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood (0-17 years) that can have lasting effects on health and well-being.
Marcia's identity status where an individual has explored alternatives and committed to a set of values/goals.
Marcia's identity status where an individual has not yet explored or committed to an identity.
Marcia's identity status where an individual has committed to an identity without exploring alternatives (often following parents' lead).
Marcia's identity status where an individual is currently exploring alternatives but has not yet made a commitment.
The psychological view that emphasizes the power of environmental forces on behavior (learning through conditioning).
A type of learning in which one learns to link two or more stimuli and anticipate events.
The process by which we learn that certain events occur together.
The initial stage in classical conditioning; the phase associating a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus.
Learning that certain events occur together. The events may be two stimuli (classical) or a response and its consequences (operant).
A stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers a response.
The unlearned, naturally occurring response to the unconditioned stimulus.
An originally irrelevant stimulus that, after association with an unconditioned stimulus, comes to trigger a conditioned response.
The learned response to a previously neutral (but now conditioned) stimulus.
The diminishing of a conditioned response; occurs when a UCS does not follow a CS.
The reappearance, after a pause, of an extinguished conditioned response.
The learned ability to distinguish between a conditioned stimulus and stimuli that do not signal an unconditioned stimulus.
The tendency, once a response has been conditioned, for stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus to elicit similar responses.
A procedure in which the conditioned stimulus in one conditioning experience is paired with a new neutral stimulus, creating a second (often weaker) conditioned stimulus.
A behavior therapy procedure that uses classical conditioning to evoke new responses to stimuli that are triggering unwanted behaviors.
A classically conditioned avoidance of a particular food that develops when an organism becomes ill after eating it.
A propensity for learning particular kinds of associations over others (e.g., taste and nausea).
Decreasing responsiveness with repeated stimulation.
A type of learning in which behavior is strengthened if followed by a reinforcer or diminished if followed by a punishment.
Any event that strengthens the behavior it follows.
An event that tends to decrease the behavior that it follows.
Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by favorable consequences become more likely, and behaviors followed by unfavorable consequences become less likely.
Increasing behaviors by presenting positive stimuli, such as food.
Increasing behaviors by stopping or reducing negative stimuli, such as shock. (It is NOT punishment).
An innately reinforcing stimulus, such as one that satisfies a biological need (e.g., food).
A stimulus that gains its reinforcing power through its association with a primary reinforcer (e.g., money).
An operant conditioning procedure in which reinforcers guide behavior toward closer and closer approximations of the desired behavior.
The tendency of learned behavior to gradually revert to biologically predisposed patterns.
The hopelessness and passive resignation an animal or human learns when unable to avoid repeated aversive events.
Reinforcing the desired response every time it occurs.
Reinforcing a response only part of the time; results in slower acquisition but greater resistance to extinction.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response only after a specified time has elapsed.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response at unpredictable time intervals.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response only after a specified number of responses.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response after an unpredictable number of responses.
The theory that we learn social behavior by observing and imitating and by being rewarded or punished (Bandura).
The process of observing and imitating a specific behavior.
A sudden realization of a problem's solution; "Aha!" moment.
Learning that occurs but is not apparent until there is an incentive to demonstrate it.
A mental representation of the layout of one's environment.
A type of learning that occurs by observing the consequences of another person's behavior
The process of explaining the causes of behavior and events.
Explaining behavior based on internal factors like personality, character, or ability.
Explaining behavior based on external factors like environment or social pressure.
A person's characteristic way of explaining negative and positive events.
Attributing failures to external, unstable, and specific causes.
Attributing failures to internal, stable, and global causes.
The tendency to attribute our own actions to external causes while attributing others' actions to internal ones.
Overestimating dispositional factors and underestimating situational factors when judging others.
Attributing personal successes to internal factors and failures to external factors.
The belief that one has personal control over their life and outcomes.
The belief that outcomes are determined by fate, luck, or outside forces.
Repeated exposure to a stimulus increases our preference for it.
A prediction that causes itself to become true due to the behavior of the believer.
Evaluating one's own abilities or opinions by comparing them to others.
Comparing ourselves to those we perceive as better off to motivate ourselves or feel inferior.
Comparing ourselves to those we perceive as worse off to boost self-esteem.
The perception that we are worse off than the people we compare ourselves to.
A generalized belief about a group of people.
The total amount of mental effort being used in working memory.
An unjustifiable and usually negative attitude toward a group and its members.
Unjustifiable negative behavior toward a group and its members.
Unconscious evaluations or feelings toward objects or people.
The tendency to believe the world is fair and people get what they deserve.
Viewing members of an out-group as all the same compared to in-group diversity.
The tendency to favor our own group over others.
The belief that one's own culture or ethnic group is superior.
Clinging to one's initial beliefs even after they have been discredited.
Searching for information that supports our preconceptions and ignoring contradictory evidence.
The tension experienced when our attitudes and behaviors do not match.
Understood rules for accepted and expected behavior in a group.
The study of how individuals' thoughts and behaviors are influenced by others.
Conforming to gain approval or avoid being disliked by a group.
Conforming because we believe others have more accurate information.
Persuasion focusing on logic, facts, and the content of the message.
Persuasion based on incidental cues like attractiveness or celebrity endorsement.
When our overall positive impression of a person influences our feelings about their specific traits.
Getting someone to agree to a large request by first getting them to agree to a small one.
Following an initial large, rejected request with a smaller, more reasonable one.
Adjusting behavior or thinking to match a group standard.
Changing behavior in response to a direct order from an authority figure.
Prioritizing personal goals and identity over group goals.
Prioritizing group goals and identity over personal ones.
The presence of several distinct cultural groups within a society.
The tendency for a group's existing beliefs to strengthen after discussion.
When the desire for group harmony overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives.
Feeling less responsible for taking action when others are present.
Exerting less effort when working in a group than when working alone.
The loss of self-awareness and self-restraint in anonymous group situations.
Improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks when others are watching.
Overestimating the degree to which others share our beliefs and behaviors.
Shared goals that override differences and require cooperation.
Situations where individuals' self-interest leads to mutually destructive behavior.
Psychologists who apply psychological principles to the workplace.
Physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged stress.
Unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
Any action intended to help others.
The feeling of being obligated to return a favor or service.
The expectation that people will help those who have helped them.
The expectation that people will help those who are dependent on them.
The finding that a person is less likely to help when others are present.
Environmental factors that influence how a person reacts in a social setting.
Factors that determine which parts of a situation a person focuses on.
Focuses on the unconscious mind and childhood experiences in shaping personality.
Mental activities below the level of conscious awareness that influence behavior.
Unconscious tactics that reduce anxiety by distorting reality.
Refusing to believe or even perceive painful realities.
Shifting aggressive impulses toward a less threatening object or person.
Attributing one's own threatening impulses to others.
Creating self-justifying explanations to hide real reasons for actions.
Switching unacceptable impulses into their opposites.
Retreating to a more infantile or comfortable stage of development.
Banishing anxiety-arousing thoughts and memories from consciousness.
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities.
Personality tests using ambiguous stimuli to reveal inner dynamics.
Information that is not currently conscious but can be easily recalled.
A reservoir of mostly unacceptable thoughts, wishes, and feelings.
Focuses on personal growth, free will, and self-actualization.
Total acceptance toward another person.
The innate drive to maintain and enhance the human organism.
Behavior is influenced by the interaction between traits and social context.
The interacting influences of behavior, internal cognition, and environment.
All our thoughts and feelings about ourselves in answer to "Who am I?"
One's belief in their ability to succeed in a specific task.
One's overall sense of self-worth or value.
Descriptions of personality based on stable and enduring behavior patterns.
A model consisting of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
Trait characterized by being cooperative, trustworthy, and good-natured.
Trait characterized by curiosity, imagination, and independence.
Trait characterized by sociability, energy, and talkativeness.
Trait characterized by organization, responsibility, and discipline.
The degree to which one is calm, secure, and self-satisfied (low Neuroticism).
Questionnaires designed to gauge a wide range of feelings and behaviors.
A statistical procedure used to identify clusters of related personality items.
Physiological needs create tension that motivates an organism to satisfy the need.
The maintenance of a steady internal state.
People are motivated to maintain an optimal level of alertness.
The perfect amount of stress or excitement needed for peak performance.
The principle that performance increases with arousal only up to a certain point.
Motivation is based on the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness.
The desire to perform a behavior for its own internal satisfaction.
Behavior is motivated by a desire for external rewards.
The desire to perform a behavior to receive external rewards or avoid punishment.
Complex, unlearned behaviors that are rigidly patterned throughout a species.
Describes internal conflicts between different types of goals.
Choosing between two desirable options.
A single option that has both positive and negative qualities.
Choosing between two undesirable options.
Motivation to seek out novel, complex, and intense experiences.
Seeking excitement through risky physical activities.
Seeking excitement through travel or non-dangerous novel experiences.
Seeking release through social extroversion and lack of restraint.
A low tolerance for routine or repetitive tasks.
A hormone secreted by an empty stomach that signals hunger.
A hormone secreted by fat cells that signals satiety (fullness).
The brain region that controls hunger, thirst, and body temperature.
The "master gland" that regulates growth and other endocrine glands.
The experience or expression of emotion or mood.
The biological and environmental causes of an emotional state.
The difference between physical arousal and the mental processing of an emotion.
The name or interpretation assigned to a physical state of arousal.
The idea that facial expressions can influence emotional experiences.
The mental interpretation of a situation that determines the emotional response.
Cultural norms that regulate the expression of emotions.
Specific triggers that cause an emotional response.
A subfield of psychology that provides psychology's contribution to behavioral medicine, focusing on how biological, social, and psychological factors influence health and illness.
The process by which we perceive and respond to certain events, called stressors, that we appraise as threatening or challenging.
High blood pressure; a physical condition often exacerbated by chronic psychological stress.
The weakening of the body's ability to fight off infection, often caused by the release of stress hormones like cortisol.
Specific events or chronic pressures that place demands on a person or threaten their well-being.
A positive form of stress that results from a challenge and can lead to increased focus, motivation, and performance.
A negative form of stress that occurs when a person feels unable to cope with demands, often leading to fatigue or health issues.
Potentially traumatic events occurring in childhood (0-17 years) that can have long-lasting effects on health and well-being.
Hans Selye's concept of the body's adaptive response to stress in three phases: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
The first stage of GAS where the sympathetic nervous system is suddenly activated (heart rate zooms, blood diverted to muscles).
The second stage of GAS where temperature, blood pressure, and respiration remain high, and the body attempts to cope with the stressor.
An involuntary physiological reaction to a perceived harmful event, attack, or threat to survival.
The third stage of GAS where the body’s resources are depleted, making the individual more vulnerable to illness or collapse.
Under stress, people (especially women) often provide support to others (tend) and bond with and seek support from others (befriend).
Attempting to alleviate stress directly by changing the stressor or the way we interact with that stressor.
Attempting to alleviate stress by avoiding or ignoring a stressor and attending to emotional needs related to one's stress reaction.
The scientific study of human flourishing, with the goals of discovering and promoting strengths and virtues that help individuals and communities to thrive.
A positive state of mental, emotional, and social functioning, characterized by life satisfaction, resilience, and a sense of purpose
The personal strength that helps most people cope with stress and recover from adversity and even trauma.
Feelings such as joy, pride, and relief that contribute to an individual's sense of well-being.
A felt sense of wonder, thankfulness, and appreciation for life and the benefits received from others.
Internal states like happiness, joy, and satisfaction with life.
Self-perceived happiness or satisfaction with life.
Character strengths that are most essential to who an individual is and that they use most naturally.
Core characteristics valued by moral philosophers and religious thinkers throughout history (e.g., wisdom, courage).
Observable positive life circumstances, such as educational attainment or stable relationships.
A state of mind or feeling characterized by contentment, love, satisfaction, pleasure, or joy.
A character strength involving the acquisition and use of knowledge.
Emotional strengths that involve the exercise of will to accomplish goals in the face of opposition.
Interpersonal strengths that involve tending and befriending others.
Civic strengths that underlie healthy community life.
Strengths that protect against excess (e.g., forgiveness, humility, prudence).
Strengths that forge connections to the larger universe and provide meaning (e.g., gratitude, hope).
Positive psychological changes as a result of struggling with extremely challenging circumstances and life crises.
Behavior that interferes with daily life and the ability to function effectively in society.
Subjective feelings of pain, anxiety, or sorrow that accompany psychological disorders.
The rules and expectations of behavior within a specific social group.
A mark of disgrace associated with a particular circumstance, quality, or person, often applied to mental illness.
Prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against someone of a different race based on the belief that one's own race is superior.
Prejudice, stereotyping, or discrimination, typically against women, on the basis of sex.
Prejudice or discrimination on the basis of a person's age.
Unjustifiable negative behavior toward a group and its members.

terms.term: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)
terms.definition: The American Psychiatric Association's system for classifying and diagnosing psychological disorders.
The World Health Organization's system for classifying diseases and health problems, including mental disorders.
An approach to psychotherapy that, depending on the client’s problems, uses techniques from various forms of therapy.
The view that psychological disorders are a result of learned behaviors through conditioning and observation.
Learned behaviors or thoughts that are dysfunctional or harmful to the individual.
The view that disorders result from unconscious conflicts and early childhood experiences.
The view that disorders arise when people are prevented from achieving self-actualization or their true potential.
The view that disorders are caused by maladaptive or irrational thought patterns.
The view that certain behaviors associated with disorders may have been adaptive for survival in our ancestors.
The view that social and cultural factors (e.g., poverty, norms) contribute to the development of psychological disorders.
The view that psychological disorders have physical causes that can be diagnosed, treated, and often cured.
An integrated approach that incorporates biological, psychological, and social-cultural levels of analysis.
The theory that a disorder results from a combination of a genetic predisposition (diathesis) and stressful life events.
Disorders that typically manifest early in development, often before the child enters grade school, and are characterized by developmental deficits.
A psychological disorder marked by extreme inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity.
A disorder that appears in childhood and is marked by significant deficiencies in communication and social interaction, and by rigidly fixated interests and repetitive behaviors.
A group of severe disorders characterized by disorganized and delusional thinking, disturbed perceptions, and inappropriate emotions and behaviors.
False beliefs, often of persecution or grandeur, that may accompany psychotic disorders.
False sensory experiences, such as seeing something in the absence of an external visual stimulus.
Fragmented or distorted thought processes, often visible through speech patterns in schizophrenia.
Speech that is incoherent and lacks a logical progression, sometimes referred to as word salad.
Unpredictable or inappropriate physical movement, ranging from childlike silliness to violent agitation.
Symptoms characterized by the absence of normal behaviors, such as a flat affect or social withdrawal.
Symptoms characterized by the presence of inappropriate behaviors, such as hallucinations or delusions.
Beliefs that others are out to get you or are plotting against you.
Beliefs that you are much more important, powerful, or wealthy than you actually are.
Jumbled ideas within a sentence that do not make sense to the listener.
A severe reduction in emotional expressiveness, often found in schizophrenia.
An immobile, expressionless, coma-like state associated with schizophrenia.
The theory that schizophrenia results from excessive activity of the neurotransmitter dopamine.
A category of disorders characterized by persistent feelings of sadness and a loss of interest in activities.
A disorder in which a person experiences two or more weeks with five or more symptoms, at least one of which must be depressed mood or loss of interest.
A mild but long-term form of depression, lasting for at least two years.
Disorders in which a person alternates between the hopelessness and lethargy of depression and the overexcited state of mania.
The transition between different mood states (mania and depression) in bipolar disorder.
A hyperactive, wildly optimistic state in which dangerously poor judgment is common.
A state of low mood and aversion to activity that can affect a person's thoughts, behavior, feelings, and sense of well-being.
A type of bipolar disorder marked by full manic episodes and usually major depressive episodes.
A type of bipolar disorder marked by hypomanic episodes and major depressive episodes.
Psychological disorders characterized by distressing, persistent anxiety or maladaptive behaviors that reduce anxiety.
An anxiety disorder marked by a persistent, irrational fear and avoidance of a specific object, activity, or situation.
Fear of heights.
Fear of spiders.
Fear or avoidance of situations, such as crowds or wide-open places, where one has felt loss of control and panic.
An anxiety disorder marked by unpredictable, minutes-long episodes of intense dread in which a person experiences terror and chest pain.
A sudden episode of intense fear that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger or apparent cause.
A cultural syndrome found primarily among Latino populations, involving intense emotional upset and physical symptoms similar to a panic attack.
Intense fear of social situations, leading to avoidance of such.
A Japanese culture-specific syndrome involving fear of offending or embarrassing others.
An anxiety disorder in which a person is continually tense, apprehensive, and in a state of autonomic nervous system arousal.
A group of disorders characterized by repetitive thoughts (obsessions) and behaviors (compulsions).
Persistent, unwanted thoughts, ideas, or images that cause distress.
Repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession.
A disorder characterized by unwanted repetitive thoughts and/or actions
Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value.
Disorders in which conscious awareness becomes separated from previous memories, thoughts, and feelings.
A disconnection between a person's thoughts, memories, feelings, actions, or sense of who they are.
A disorder characterized by an inability to recall important personal information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature.
A rare dissociative disorder in which a person exhibits two or more distinct and alternating personalities.
A category of disorders where exposure to a traumatic or stressful event is listed explicitly as a diagnostic criterion.
An enhanced state of sensory sensitivity accompanied by an exaggerated intensity of behaviors whose purpose is to detect threats.
Vivid, involuntary reliving of a traumatic event.
Persistent problems in falling or staying asleep, often associated with trauma or stress.
An inability to connect with others on an emotional level, common in PTSD.
A state of ill will or unfriendliness, sometimes manifesting in trauma-related disorders.
A disorder characterized by haunting memories, nightmares, social withdrawal, jumpy anxiety, and/or insomnia that lingers for four weeks or more after a traumatic experience.
Disorders characterized by persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behavior that results in altered consumption or absorption of food.
An eating disorder in which a person maintains a starvation diet despite being significantly underweight.
An eating disorder in which a person alternates binge eating with purging or fasting.
Inflexible and enduring behavior patterns that impair social functioning.
A group of personality disorders including Paranoid, Schizoid, and Schizotypal.
Characterized by pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others.
Characterized by detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotional expression.
Characterized by acute discomfort in close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, and eccentricities of behavior.

terms.term: Cluster B (dramatic, emotional, or erratic cluster)
terms.definition: A group of personality disorders including Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, and Narcissistic.
A personality disorder in which a person exhibits a lack of conscience for wrongdoing, even toward friends and family members.
Characterized by excessive emotionality and attention seeking.
Characterized by a long-term pattern of abnormal feelings of self-importance and an excessive need for admiration.
Characterized by instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, and marked impulsivity.
A group of personality disorders including Avoidant, Dependent, and Obsessive-Compulsive.
Characterized by social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation.
Characterized by a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behavior.
Characterized by a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control.
Clinical decision-making that integrates the best available research with clinical expertise and patient characteristics and preferences.
An ability to maintain an interpersonal stance that is other-oriented (or open to the other) in relation to aspects of cultural identity that are most important to the client.
A bond of trust and mutual understanding between a therapist and client, who work together constructively to overcome the client’s problem.
Drugs that affect mental processes, such as mind, emotions, and behavior.
The ethical principle of "doing no harm" to the patient.
The ethical principle of being loyal and keeping promises to the client.
The ethical principle of being honest and truthful in the practice of psychology.

terms.term: Respect for people’s rights and dignity
terms.definition: The ethical principle of respecting the autonomy and privacy of individuals.
Therapy deriving from the psychoanalytic tradition that views individuals as responding to unconscious forces and childhood experiences.
A method of exploring the unconscious in which the person relaxes and says whatever comes to mind, no matter how trivial or embarrassing.
A technique used in psychoanalysis to reveal unconscious conflicts by analyzing the content of dreams.
Therapy that teaches people new, more adaptive ways of thinking; based on the assumption that thoughts intervene between events and our emotional reactions.
A therapeutic process of learning to identify and dispute irrational or maladaptive thoughts.
A list of feared situations ordered from least to most anxiety-provoking, used in systematic desensitization.
The process of replacing negative or distorted thoughts with realistic and positive ones.
Aaron Beck’s theory that depression is caused by negative views of the self, the world, and the future.
The use of specific techniques and principles to bring about meaningful and positive change in behavior, often used with ASD.
Behavioral techniques that treat anxieties by having people experience (in a controlled way) that which they fear
A type of exposure therapy that associates a pleasant relaxed state with gradually increasing anxiety-triggering stimuli.
A type of counterconditioning that associates an unpleasant state (such as nausea) with an unwanted behavior (such as drinking alcohol).
An operant conditioning procedure in which people earn a token of some sort for exhibiting a desired behavior and can later exchange the tokens for various privileges or treats.
A system for electronically recording, amplifying, and feeding back information regarding a subtle physiological state, such as blood pressure or muscle tension.
A popular integrative therapy that combines cognitive therapy (changing self-defeating thinking) with behavior therapy (changing behavior).
A form of CBT used to treat Borderline Personality Disorder, focusing on mindfulness and emotional regulation.
A confrontational cognitive therapy, developed by Albert Ellis, that vigorously challenges people’s illogical, self-defeating attitudes and assumptions.
A humanistic therapy, developed by Carl Rogers, in which the therapist uses techniques such as active listening within a genuine, accepting, empathic environment.
Empathic listening in which the listener echoes, restates, and clarifies.
A caring, accepting, nonjudgmental attitude, which Carl Rogers believed would help clients develop self-awareness and self-acceptance.
Therapy conducted with groups rather than individuals, permitting therapeutic benefits from group interaction.
A social interaction in which one person suggests to another that certain perceptions, feelings, thoughts, or behaviors will spontaneously occur.
Chemicals that affect the central nervous system and alter activity in the brain.
Drugs used to treat depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD (most commonly SSRIs).
Drugs used to control anxiety and agitation.
A chemical that provides an effective drug therapy for the mood swings of bipolar disorder.
Drugs used to treat schizophrenia and other forms of severe thought disorder.
Involuntary movements of the facial muscles, tongue, and limbs; a possible neurotoxic side effect of long-term use of antipsychotic drugs.
Surgery that removes or destroys brain tissue in an effort to change behavior.
The purposeful removal or destruction of part of the brain.
The application of repeated pulses of magnetic energy to the brain; used to stimulate or suppress brain activity.
A biomedical therapy for severely depressed patients in which a brief electric current is sent through the brain of an anesthetized patient.
A psychosurgical procedure once used to calm uncontrollably emotional or violent patients by cutting the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the emotion-controlling centers of the inner brain.
